title: Docker and containers
idea: Docker packages an app and everything it needs to run into an image. A container runs that image in isolation, on a machine with Docker.

analogy.text: A shipping container. Goods are packed once into a standard box, and any ship, train or truck can carry it without unpacking.
analogy.breaks: Linux containers still need Linux underneath, even on a Mac.

points: A container is an isolated process with its own files and network.
Containers share the host's kernel, the core of its operating system.
Containers are lightweight, so one host can run many at once.
Teams ship the same tested image from a laptop to production.

steps.caption: You package the Book Store API, Node.js and its packages into one image.
A machine with Docker can start a container from the image. Here, your laptop does.
The test server gets the same image and starts its own container.
Production does the same. Node.js and the packages are identical on all three machines.
Each host runs its own container. The image itself never changes.

code.caption: The whole workflow in three commands, run on any machine that has Docker and the project.

walk.text: Build an image named `bookstore-api` from the recipe in `Dockerfile`.
Start a container named `api` from it, in the background. Later pages explain each flag.
Call the API through port 3000 on your own machine.

takeaway: Docker turns installing an app into starting a container.

starters: Is Docker the same as a virtual machine?
